Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

Very important: Prop 3 (make high-income tax rates permanent, $5-15B/year, supported by teachers) is polling at 54-58% yes — well above Prop 41's 38-48%. So Prop 3 would likely outpoll Prop 41, meaning Prop 41's nullification clause wouldn't void Prop 3 (Prop 3 gets more affirmative votes). But Prop 41's ongoing audit requirements could still apply to Prop 3's programs if Prop 3 is deemed "enacted on or after January 1, 2026" — a legal risk. Also the conflicting measures clause in Prop 41 says "In the event that this initiative measure receives a greater number of affirmative votes, the provisions of this measure shall prevail in their entirety, and all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void." So if Prop 3 gets more votes, Prop 3 prevails on conflicts — but Prop 41's non-conflicting provisions still apply (per the constitution's general rule, conflicting provisions only). Actually Prop 41's clause says all provisions of the other measure are null and void if Prop 41 receives greater votes — that's harsher than the constitutional default (which nullifies only conflicting provisions). If Prop 3 receives more votes, then per constitution, Prop 3 prevails on conflicting provisions.

Key downside risks of Prop 41 if passed:
1. Would nullify Prop 40 if Prop 40 passes with fewer yes votes than Prop 41 — eliminating ~$100B health care funding intended to backfill federal cuts. But polls show Prop 40 is likely to fail outright (46% support). If Prop 40 fails, this is moot. But there's a scenario where Prop 40 passes (say 51%) and Prop 41 passes (52%). Then Prop 41 wins → billionaire tax void.

Interesting strategic consideration: If a voter supports Prop 40 (the billionaire tax), they should vote No on 41. If a voter opposes Prop 40, voting yes on 41 is a backstop but unnecessary if 40 fails.

2. Long-term constraints: prohibits exclusion of new state taxes from the Gann limit; risk of invalidating or complicating MCO tax (Prop 35 uses limit increase), HQAF, SNF-QAF, SB 125 audits → billions in federal Medi-Cal matching funds at risk (per legal scholars and Budget Center). Also could chill future special-tax initiatives with costly, slanted pre-election audits (must recommend 10% cost cuts and private-sector comparisons), with the audit summary placed prominently in the VIG right after the LAO analysis.

3. Burdens the State Auditor with mandatory audits triggered at only 25% of signatures — the office has limited capacity; costs to General Fund for failed initiatives.

4. Retroactive application to Jan 1, 2026, creating legal uncertainty for taxes enacted in 2026 (SB 125 MCO tax, HQAF reauthorization).

5. It's a constitutional amendment that the Legislature can't fix (2/3 + voters), with a "liberal construction" clause and self-defense provision funding independent counsel — unusual and reducing democratic flexibility.

6. Deceptive single-subject issue: packaged "good government" veneer with a targeted poison pill; nearly all major newspapers (SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, LA Times Skelton, Mercury News, San Diego UT?) recommend No. SPUR: No. LWV: No. California Democratic Party: No. Opposed by Bernie Sanders, SEIU-UHW.

Supporters: CalChamber, Howard Jarvis, Reform California, CalCPA, CalTax, former State Auditor Tom Hayes, Steve Westly, Hoover Institution (leaning favorable analysis), San Luis Obispo Tribune (yes).

Weighing: The merits of the audit idea are modest and largely duplicative; the Gann limit lock has serious, poorly-understood risks to health care financing and future revenue measures; the measure's principal purpose is to kill a specific tax via a hidden clause, and it's overwhelmingly funded by billionaires who would pay that tax. It's polling below majority (38% yes/47% no IGS; 48% PPIC). The preponderance of independent, nonpartisan analyses (LAO flags unknown fiscal effects; Budget Center; LWV; SPUR; most editorial boards) points to No.

However, let me consider the counterargument seriously. If a voter believes the billionaire tax is bad policy (many economists do, including left-leaning ones worried about capital flight; Governor Newsom, CTA, CMA oppose it), then Prop 41 serves as insurance. But that voter can simply vote No on Prop 40 — which directly accomplishes that. Prop 41's added value is only in the scenario where Prop 40 narrowly passes with fewer votes than Prop 41. Meanwhile, Prop 41's permanent structural costs apply regardless. So a No vote on 41 combined with a No on 40 achieves the same immediate goal without the long-term damage. And a Yes on 40 voter definitely wants No on 41.

Therefore, "no" is the better answer under both preference profiles, unless the voter wants the Gann limit lock and audit regime for its own sake. Given the drafting quality concerns and the risk to Medi-Cal financing (MCO tax/HQAF draw federal matching dollars worth ~$8-19B/yr), the expected-value answer is no.

Let me double check a couple of facts: (a) that Prop 35's MCO tax used Art. XIII B Sec. 4 limit increase (yes, per memo); (b) Prop 41's Sec 4(b)(2) defines exemption to include "The appropriations limit for the State of California is increased by statute pursuant to Section 4 of Article XIII B" — and Sec 3(b) says the state shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax enacted/taking effect on or after Jan 1, 2026 if exempted/excluded. Prop 35's MCO tax takes effect in 2027 and relies on a statutory limit increase → risk it becomes uncollectable. That's a substantial risk noted by both the tax professors and the California Budget & Policy Center. Even the Hoover analysis notes Gann limit is not currently binding ($30B headroom), so the "discipline" benefit is speculative while the risks are concrete.

Also check whether the Yes campaign has responded to the MCO/HQAF concerns. Let me search quickly for the Yes on 41 campaign's response and any legal rebuttal (e.g., Loren Kaye). Also check whether the LAO addressed the MCO tax risk in its analysis of the initiative. That would strengthen the assessment. Let me do one more round of research.

XIII B Sec. 4 limit increase (yes, per memo); (b) Prop 41's Sec 4(b)(2) defines exemption to include "The appropriations limit for the State of California is increased by statute pursuant to Section 4 of Article XIII B" — and Sec 3(b) says the state shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax enacted/taking effect on or after Jan 1, 2026 if exempted/excluded. 5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)
October 5, 2026 October 4, 2026
Republish
Share this:

Mayra Joseph, a teacher at Sylvia Mendez Elementary School in Berkeley, joined members of the California Teachers Association and supporters of public education in a march to the Capitol as part of RedForEd Day of Action in Sacramento on May 22, 2019. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Δ
Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:03 PM PST | UPDATED: November 3, 2026 at 4:35 AM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Related Articles
Election Day: Five things to watch for in California (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/03/election-day-five-things-to-watch-for-in-california-2/)
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
Prop. 40 also exempts itself from the state spending limit, so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. Prop. 41 makes sure measures like Prop. 40 can’t rip off taxpayers and schools by exempting themselves from the state spending limit.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:03 PM PST | UPDATED: November 3, 2026 at 4:35 AM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Related Articles
Election Day: Five things to watch for in California (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/03/election-day-five-things-to-watch-for-in-california-2/)
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.

California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
Prop. 40 also exempts itself from the state spending limit, so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. Prop. 41 makes sure measures like Prop. 40 can’t rip off taxpayers and schools by exempting themselves from the state spending limit.

Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.
What is the biggest logical error opponents of Prop. 41 make?
Prop. 41’s opponents are all proponents of more taxes and more spending regardless of the accountability, oversight, transparency or trackable metrics needed to help improve the results we get for our tax dollars.
The California State Auditor’s Office is absolutely first-rate and does a fantastic job providing unbiased, nonpartisan, objective information. Getting this type of information to voters, both as part of the Voter Guide and on an ongoing basis (for taxes that are approved), is something that we should have done long ago.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
Voters support the idea of more transparency and accountability. Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop. 41:
“Q: this measure would require the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new taxes. Knowing this, do you support or oppose this proposal?”

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:05 PM PST | UPDATED: November 3, 2026 at 4:34 AM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What’s the strongest argument against Prop. 41?
Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share in taxes. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
One of Prop. 41’s main funders is Google founder Sergey Brin, whose wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion. Now he’s spent tens of millions of dollars to fund this sham measure that attempts to cancel out the billionaire tax.
But Prop. 41 isn’t just a scheme, it’s an expensive one. It would require pre-election and ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by new special taxes, costing the state time and money. California already has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor who regularly issues reports on state operations.
This initiative isn’t about helping Californians — it’s about billionaires avoiding a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
Don’t voters deserve an unbiased look at how their money will be spent before they vote on a new tax?
California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. Prop. 41 goes beyond providing voters with information. It requires a pre-election audit of programs that would receive special-tax revenue, which isn’t only not possible, it interferes with the existing authority of the state auditor.
In addition, any change in audit rules should not undermine the only viable response to $100 billion in federal health care cuts under H.R. 1. Prop. 40 would use funds generated by the billionaire tax to keep hospitals and ERs open, as well as fund health care services that Californians count on like Medicaid and marketplace coverage under the Affordable Care Act. These are all programs that California taxpayers currently fund, and that the Trump administration cut by $100 billion dollars over the next five years. Prop. 40 would backfill those cuts.
What is wrong with forcing government programs to find 10% in cost savings to protect taxpayer dollars?
There’s nothing wrong with finding genuine savings and improving services that California taxpayers support and rely upon. The problem with Prop. 41 is that that is the role of the state auditor, not Sergey Brin.
Prop. 41 doesn’t simply require programs to identify waste. Its audit framework specifically requires recommendations for achieving at least 10% annual budgetary savings and comparisons with analogous private-sector programs.
Those are very different things.
A program may be expensive because the service itself is expensive — not because 10% of its funding is wasted. That’s particularly important for health care, where costs can reflect the escalating costs of prescription drugs, a rapidly aging population, provider shortages and changing federal requirements.
A good government should identify waste, fraud and inefficiency. But that requires evidence, not an arbitrary savings target imposed across fundamentally different programs.
You argue this is a strategy by billionaires to avoid paying taxes. Can you explain exactly how Prop. 41 would block the Prop. 40 wealth tax?
Yes, it hinges on Prop. 41’s Gann Limit provision.
Prop. 41 prohibits collecting state taxes enacted or taking effect after January 1, 2026 if they rely on an exemption or exclusion from the state’s Gann spending limit, which Prop. 40 does.
That’s important because Prop. 40 is a special tax initiative with revenues dedicated to health care services. Without the ability to structure the tax and its spending outside the Gann Limit, the estimated revenue of $100 billion cannot be spent as voters intended.
Prop. 41 creates a new constitutional restriction that directly conflicts with the fiscal structure Prop. 40 requires. Exceptions to the Gann limit are common, and the Gann limit itself, which ties the government to what it spent and prioritized in 1979, is just poor public policy.
If Prop. 41 fails, how else do you suggest California ensure that special tax revenues are being spent efficiently?
California already has mechanisms to do that. The state has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor that regularly examines state operations and issues public reports. We should use and strengthen those mechanisms where necessary. The better approach is targeted oversight: audit programs, evaluate outcomes, identify waste or fraud, publish the findings and hold policymakers accountable.
Why should people opposed to Prop. 40 also vote against Prop. 41?
Because Prop. 41 is not limited to Prop. 40. Prop. 41 is likely to endanger other revenue measures, including education funding, taxes connected to Medi-Cal and other health care financing mechanisms.
For instance, Prop. 41 could subject Prop. 3 — the education-funding measure — to its new audit rules. If Prop. 41 receives more votes, it could thereby put Prop. 3’s tax extension at risk of being struck down because of the conflicting language. It could also similarly threaten Medi-Cal taxes and fees that bring the state billions of dollars in federal matching funds.
So someone can oppose Prop. 40 on its merits and still conclude that Prop. 41 goes too far.
If voters don’t like the goals of Prop. 40, they can vote against it. There is no reason to change the state’s constitutional rules for every future special-tax initiative .
Why should people who want the state government to carefully scrutinize how tax dollars are spent still vote against Prop. 41?
Because scrutiny already exists, and Prop. 41 isn’t a carefully written, thoughtful ballot measure. It’s a reckless and dangerous initiative that could undo Prop. 40 and wreak havoc with other taxpayer-funded initiatives that have already been approved by taxpayers. As we’ve shared above, California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. If voters are concerned about existing state programs, they can demand better oversight by the auditor and policymakers.
Why shouldn’t programs funded by special taxes face a mandatory check-up every four years to ensure the money isn’t being wasted?
There’s nothing inherently wrong with reviewing programs every four years. The problem is what Prop. 41 requires those reviews to do. They aren’t simply performance check-ups. The audits must examine comparisons with imaginary “private-sector programs” which don’t exist in the case of Medicaid and marketplace insurance coverage.
In addition, Medicaid is one of the most efficient forms of health care coverage (https://healthlaw.org/medicaid-is-even-leaner-as-accountability-improves/) in this country, and 1 in 5 of Californians count on it for their health care. This includes children, people with disabilities, seniors and many veterans.
While federal health care programs can always be strengthened and improved, the most urgent issue facing Californians right now is ensuring billionaires pay their fair share to keep local hospitals and ERs open and health care affordable for millions of working people.
What is the biggest logical error proponents of Prop. 41 make?
They are counting on the fact that California voters won’t see through their poison pill ballot measure, which we believe they will. Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
This initiative isn’t about helping California taxpayers — it’s about defeating one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they would rather millions of working people lose health care than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
In short, Prop. 41 would insert constitutional barriers in the way of future voters trying to fund health care, education and other public priorities just because Sergy Brin doesn’t want to pay a modest 5% tax on his vast wealth. Instead, he’d like to shift the cost of keeping hospitals, ERs and clinics open onto ordinary taxpayers, who already pay higher effective tax rates than billionaires do.
Prop. 41 is deceptive, dangerous, deeply unfair, and we believe California voters will vote “no” on this measure.

Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.

Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.
What is the biggest logical error opponents of Prop. 41 make?
Prop. 41’s opponents are all proponents of more taxes and more spending regardless of the accountability, oversight, transparency or trackable metrics needed to help improve the results we get for our tax dollars.
The California State Auditor’s Office is absolutely first-rate and does a fantastic job providing unbiased, nonpartisan, objective information. Getting this type of information to voters, both as part of the Voter Guide and on an ongoing basis (for taxes that are approved), is something that we should have done long ago.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
Voters support the idea of more transparency and accountability. Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop. 41:
“Q: this measure would require the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new taxes. Knowing this, do you support or oppose this proposal?”
