What’s the strongest argument against Prop. 41?
Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share in taxes. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
One of Prop. 41’s main funders is Google founder Sergey Brin, whose wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion. Now he’s spent tens of millions of dollars to fund this sham measure that attempts to cancel out the billionaire tax.
But Prop. 41 isn’t just a scheme, it’s an expensive one. It would require pre-election and ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by new special taxes, costing the state time and money. California already has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor who regularly issues reports on state operations.
This initiative isn’t about helping Californians — it’s about billionaires avoiding a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
Don’t voters deserve an unbiased look at how their money will be spent before they vote on a new tax?
California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. Prop. 41 goes beyond providing voters with information. It requires a pre-election audit of programs that would receive special-tax revenue, which isn’t only not possible, it interferes with the existing authority of the state auditor.
In addition, any change in audit rules should not undermine the only viable response to $100 billion in federal health care cuts under H.R. 1. Prop. 40 would use funds generated by the billionaire tax to keep hospitals and ERs open, as well as fund health care services that Californians count on like Medicaid and marketplace coverage under the Affordable Care Act. These are all programs that California taxpayers currently fund, and that the Trump administration cut by $100 billion dollars over the next five years. Prop. 40 would backfill those cuts.
What is wrong with forcing government programs to find 10% in cost savings to protect taxpayer dollars?
There’s nothing wrong with finding genuine savings and improving services that California taxpayers support and rely upon. The problem with Prop. 41 is that that is the role of the state auditor, not Sergey Brin.
Prop. 41 doesn’t simply require programs to identify waste. Its audit framework specifically requires recommendations for achieving at least 10% annual budgetary savings and comparisons with analogous private-sector programs.
Those are very different things.
A program may be expensive because the service itself is expensive — not because 10% of its funding is wasted. That’s particularly important for health care, where costs can reflect the escalating costs of prescription drugs, a rapidly aging population, provider shortages and changing federal requirements.
A good government should identify waste, fraud and inefficiency. But that requires evidence, not an arbitrary savings target imposed across fundamentally different programs.
You argue this is a strategy by billionaires to avoid paying taxes. Can you explain exactly how Prop. 41 would block the Prop. 40 wealth tax?
Yes, it hinges on Prop. 41’s Gann Limit provision.
Prop. 41 prohibits collecting state taxes enacted or taking effect after January 1, 2026 if they rely on an exemption or exclusion from the state’s Gann spending limit, which Prop. 40 does.
That’s important because Prop. 40 is a special tax initiative with revenues dedicated to health care services. Without the ability to structure the tax and its spending outside the Gann Limit, the estimated revenue of $100 billion cannot be spent as voters intended.
Prop. 41 creates a new constitutional restriction that directly conflicts with the fiscal structure Prop. 40 requires. Exceptions to the Gann limit are common, and the Gann limit itself, which ties the government to what it spent and prioritized in 1979, is just poor public policy.
If Prop. 41 fails, how else do you suggest California ensure that special tax revenues are being spent efficiently?
California already has mechanisms to do that. The state has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor that regularly examines state operations and issues public reports. We should use and strengthen those mechanisms where necessary. The better approach is targeted oversight: audit programs, evaluate outcomes, identify waste or fraud, publish the findings and hold policymakers accountable.
Why should people opposed to Prop. 40 also vote against Prop. 41?
Because Prop. 41 is not limited to Prop. 40. Prop. 41 is likely to endanger other revenue measures, including education funding, taxes connected to Medi-Cal and other health care financing mechanisms.
For instance, Prop. 41 could subject Prop. 3 — the education-funding measure — to its new audit rules. If Prop. 41 receives more votes, it could thereby put Prop. 3’s tax extension at risk of being struck down because of the conflicting language. It could also similarly threaten Medi-Cal taxes and fees that bring the state billions of dollars in federal matching funds.
So someone can oppose Prop. 40 on its merits and still conclude that Prop. 41 goes too far.
If voters don’t like the goals of Prop. 40, they can vote against it. There is no reason to change the state’s constitutional rules for every future special-tax initiative .
Why should people who want the state government to carefully scrutinize how tax dollars are spent still vote against Prop. 41?
Because scrutiny already exists, and Prop. 41 isn’t a carefully written, thoughtful ballot measure. It’s a reckless and dangerous initiative that could undo Prop. 40 and wreak havoc with other taxpayer-funded initiatives that have already been approved by taxpayers. As we’ve shared above, California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. If voters are concerned about existing state programs, they can demand better oversight by the auditor and policymakers.
Why shouldn’t programs funded by special taxes face a mandatory check-up every four years to ensure the money isn’t being wasted?
There’s nothing inherently wrong with reviewing programs every four years. The problem is what Prop. 41 requires those reviews to do. They aren’t simply performance check-ups. The audits must examine comparisons with imaginary “private-sector programs” which don’t exist in the case of Medicaid and marketplace insurance coverage.
In addition, Medicaid is one of the most efficient forms of health care coverage (https://healthlaw.org/medicaid-is-even-leaner-as-accountability-improves/) in this country, and 1 in 5 of Californians count on it for their health care. This includes children, people with disabilities, seniors and many veterans.
While federal health care programs can always be strengthened and improved, the most urgent issue facing Californians right now is ensuring billionaires pay their fair share to keep local hospitals and ERs open and health care affordable for millions of working people.
What is the biggest logical error proponents of Prop. 41 make?
They are counting on the fact that California voters won’t see through their poison pill ballot measure, which we believe they will. Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
This initiative isn’t about helping California taxpayers — it’s about defeating one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they would rather millions of working people lose health care than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
In short, Prop. 41 would insert constitutional barriers in the way of future voters trying to fund health care, education and other public priorities just because Sergy Brin doesn’t want to pay a modest 5% tax on his vast wealth. Instead, he’d like to shift the cost of keeping hospitals, ERs and clinics open onto ordinary taxpayers, who already pay higher effective tax rates than billionaires do.
Prop. 41 is deceptive, dangerous, deeply unfair, and we believe California voters will vote “no” on this measure.

This includes children, people with disabilities, seniors and many veterans.
While federal health care programs can always be strengthened and improved, the most urgent issue facing Californians right now is ensuring billionaires pay their fair share to keep local hospitals and ERs open and health care affordable for millions of working people.
What is the biggest logical error proponents of Prop. 41 make?
They are counting on the fact that California voters won’t see through their poison pill ballot measure, which we believe they will. Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
This initiative isn’t about helping California taxpayers — it’s about defeating one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they would rather millions of working people lose health care than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
In short, Prop. 41 would insert constitutional barriers in the way of future voters trying to fund health care, education and other public priorities just because Sergy Brin doesn’t want to pay a modest 5% tax on his vast wealth. Instead, he’d like to shift the cost of keeping hospitals, ERs and clinics open onto ordinary taxpayers, who already pay higher effective tax rates than billionaires do.
Prop. 41 is deceptive, dangerous, deeply unfair, and we believe California voters will vote “no” on this measure.

f how it operates?
Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.
What is the biggest logical error opponents of Prop. 41 make?
Prop. 41’s opponents are all proponents of more taxes and more spending regardless of the accountability, oversight, transparency or trackable metrics needed to help improve the results we get for our tax dollars.
The California State Auditor’s Office is absolutely first-rate and does a fantastic job providing unbiased, nonpartisan, objective information. Getting this type of information to voters, both as part of the Voter Guide and on an ongoing basis (for taxes that are approved), is something that we should have done long ago.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
Voters support the idea of more transparency and accountability. Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop. 41:
“Q: this measure would require the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new taxes. Knowing this, do you support or oppose this proposal?”

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What’s the strongest argument against Prop. 41?
Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share in taxes. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
One of Prop. 41’s main funders is Google founder Sergey Brin, whose wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion. Now he’s spent tens of millions of dollars to fund this sham measure that attempts to cancel out the billionaire tax.
But Prop. 41 isn’t just a scheme, it’s an expensive one. It would require pre-election and ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by new special taxes, costing the state time and money. California already has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor who regularly issues reports on state operations.
This initiative isn’t about helping Californians — it’s about billionaires avoiding a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
Don’t voters deserve an unbiased look at how their money will be spent before they vote on a new tax?
California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. Prop. 41 goes beyond providing voters with information. It requires a pre-election audit of programs that would receive special-tax revenue, which isn’t only not possible, it interferes with the existing authority of the state auditor.
In addition, any change in audit rules should not undermine the only viable response to $100 billion in federal health care cuts under H.R. 1. Prop. 40 would use funds generated by the billionaire tax to keep hospitals and ERs open, as well as fund health care services that Californians count on like Medicaid and marketplace coverage under the Affordable Care Act. These are all programs that California taxpayers currently fund, and that the Trump administration cut by $100 billion dollars over the next five years. Prop. 40 would backfill those cuts.
What is wrong with forcing government programs to find 10% in cost savings to protect taxpayer dollars?
There’s nothing wrong with finding genuine savings and improving services that California taxpayers support and rely upon. The problem with Prop. 41 is that that is the role of the state auditor, not Sergey Brin.
Prop. 41 doesn’t simply require programs to identify waste. Its audit framework specifically requires recommendations for achieving at least 10% annual budgetary savings and comparisons with analogous private-sector programs.
Those are very different things.
A program may be expensive because the service itself is expensive — not because 10% of its funding is wasted. That’s particularly important for health care, where costs can reflect the escalating costs of prescription drugs, a rapidly aging population, provider shortages and changing federal requirements.
A good government should identify waste, fraud and inefficiency. But that requires evidence, not an arbitrary savings target imposed across fundamentally different programs.
You argue this is a strategy by billionaires to avoid paying taxes. Can you explain exactly how Prop. 41 would block the Prop. 40 wealth tax?
Yes, it hinges on Prop. 41’s Gann Limit provision.
Prop. 41 prohibits collecting state taxes enacted or taking effect after January 1, 2026 if they rely on an exemption or exclusion from the state’s Gann spending limit, which Prop. 40 does.
That’s important because Prop. 40 is a special tax initiative with revenues dedicated to health care services. Without the ability to structure the tax and its spending outside the Gann Limit, the estimated revenue of $100 billion cannot be spent as voters intended.
Prop. 41 creates a new constitutional restriction that directly conflicts with the fiscal structure Prop. 40 requires. Exceptions to the Gann limit are common, and the Gann limit itself, which ties the government to what it spent and prioritized in 1979, is just poor public policy.
If Prop. 41 fails, how else do you suggest California ensure that special tax revenues are being spent efficiently?
California already has mechanisms to do that. The state has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor that regularly examines state operations and issues public reports. We should use and strengthen those mechanisms where necessary. The better approach is targeted oversight: audit programs, evaluate outcomes, identify waste or fraud, publish the findings and hold policymakers accountable.
Why should people opposed to Prop. 40 also vote against Prop. 41?
Because Prop. 41 is not limited to Prop. 40. Prop. 41 is likely to endanger other revenue measures, including education funding, taxes connected to Medi-Cal and other health care financing mechanisms.
For instance, Prop. 41 could subject Prop. 3 — the education-funding measure — to its new audit rules. If Prop. 41 receives more votes, it could thereby put Prop. 3’s tax extension at risk of being struck down because of the conflicting language. It could also similarly threaten Medi-Cal taxes and fees that bring the state billions of dollars in federal matching funds.
So someone can oppose Prop. 40 on its merits and still conclude that Prop. 41 goes too far.
If voters don’t like the goals of Prop. 40, they can vote against it. There is no reason to change the state’s constitutional rules for every future special-tax initiative .
Why should people who want the state government to carefully scrutinize how tax dollars are spent still vote against Prop. 41?
Because scrutiny already exists, and Prop. 41 isn’t a carefully written, thoughtful ballot measure. It’s a reckless and dangerous initiative that could undo Prop. 40 and wreak havoc with other taxpayer-funded initiatives that have already been approved by taxpayers. As we’ve shared above, California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. If voters are concerned about existing state programs, they can demand better oversight by the auditor and policymakers.
Why shouldn’t programs funded by special taxes face a mandatory check-up every four years to ensure the money isn’t being wasted?
There’s nothing inherently wrong with reviewing programs every four years. The problem is what Prop. 41 requires those reviews to do. They aren’t simply performance check-ups. The audits must examine comparisons with imaginary “private-sector programs” which don’t exist in the case of Medicaid and marketplace insurance coverage.
In addition, Medicaid is one of the most efficient forms of health care coverage (https://healthlaw.org/medicaid-is-even-leaner-as-accountability-improves/) in this country, and 1 in 5 of Californians count on it for their health care. This includes children, people with disabilities, seniors and many veterans.
While federal health care programs can always be strengthened and improved, the most urgent issue facing Californians right now is ensuring billionaires pay their fair share to keep local hospitals and ERs open and health care affordable for millions of working people.
What is the biggest logical error proponents of Prop. 41 make?
They are counting on the fact that California voters won’t see through their poison pill ballot measure, which we believe they will. Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
This initiative isn’t about helping California taxpayers — it’s about defeating one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they would rather millions of working people lose health care than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
In short, Prop. 41 would insert constitutional barriers in the way of future voters trying to fund health care, education and other public priorities just because Sergy Brin doesn’t want to pay a modest 5% tax on his vast wealth. Instead, he’d like to shift the cost of keeping hospitals, ERs and clinics open onto ordinary taxpayers, who already pay higher effective tax rates than billionaires do.
Prop. 41 is deceptive, dangerous, deeply unfair, and we believe California voters will vote “no” on this measure.

I now have both sides well documented. Let me consider one more dimension: is there a case that Prop 41's Gann limit lock is actually good policy? Some fiscal conservatives argue it restores discipline; the state is currently $30B under the limit so it wouldn't bind immediately. But the risks: (a) it could make health-care provider taxes/fees uncollectable (MCO tax via Prop 35's limit increase; HQAF and SNF-QAF are constitutionally excluded from the limit), jeopardizing billions in federal matching funds — a real risk flagged by both the Budget Center and law professors; (b) it could be applied to Prop 3, and its conflicting-measure clause could void Prop 3 entirely if Prop 41 outpolls Prop 3 (though Prop 3 is polling 10-16 points higher than Prop 41, making that scenario unlikely); (c) it constrains future fiscal flexibility permanently via constitutional amendment that can't be amended by the Legislature; (d) the audit regime adds cost and imposes a slanted framework on ballot measures.

Also worth noting: the measure's design is transparently targeted ("SEC. 5: This article applies to all statewide initiative measures submitted to the electors on or after January 1, 2026, including measures that appear on the ballot at the same election at which the measure adding this article is approved"). And the funding: $58M reported to the yes committee, plus >$180M spent by Building a Better California across 41/42; nearly all from billionaires who would be directly liable under Prop 40. Massive conflict of interest and asymmetric spending ($351M+ total, ~90% against the wealth tax).

Consider also that Prop 41's most consequential provision (Gann limit lock) isn't reflected in the "audits" framing used by the Yes campaign — the official title does mention it, but the campaign's own ads and arguments focus on audits. That's a deceptive framing issue (as multiple editorial boards found).

Voter decision analysis:
- If you support Prop 40: vote No on 41 (necessary to avoid nullification).
- If you oppose Prop 40: you can simply vote No on Prop 40; Prop 41's marginal benefit is insurance against Prop 40 narrowly passing with fewer votes. But it carries permanent structural risks. Expected value: The permanent harms (health-care financing risk, initiative-process burden, loss of flexibility) likely exceed the insurance value, especially since Prop 40 is polling below 50%.
- If you're a fiscal conservative who wants the Gann limit lock, yes might appeal; but even the Mercury News/Bay Area News Group and McClatchy and SF Chronicle boards (some of which are center-right on fiscal issues) recommended No on 41 largely due to the shackling effect. HJTA, Reform CA, CalChamber, San Luis Obispo Tribune recommend yes.

Given the weight of independent analysis (LAO uncertain net effect; SPUR no; LWV no; CA Budget & Policy Center no; SF Chronicle no; McClatchy/Bee/Mercury News no; LA Times columnist no; legal scholars flagging serious risks to Medi-Cal financing and Prop 3), versus the yes side (taxpayer groups, business groups, funded overwhelmingly by billionaires with a direct financial interest), my recommendation is no.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. The Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide (VIG).
Voter Initiative Process. California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process. Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot. State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot. Supporters notify the Secretary of State once they have gathered 25 percent of the necessary signatures.
Special Taxes. State taxes can be raised by the Legislature or by voters. When a “special tax” is created, the revenue from that tax is dedicated to a specific purpose or program. For example, certain fuel taxes can only be used to pay for public roads and other transportation programs.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments follow the law, use money, and run their programs. These reviews are called audits. An audit may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly over time while other audits are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process. This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit. If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG. If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.
Ongoing Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From New or Increased Special Taxes. Proposition 41 also requires the State Auditor to periodically review programs that receive funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. These ongoing audits would happen every four years. Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor will include in these audits, including recommendations to improve program efficiency. Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of this ongoing work will be paid using the new tax revenue.
State Appropriations Limit. The State Constitution limits how much tax revenues the state can spend each year. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes and special taxes. However, certain types of spending, for example for infrastructure, are excluded from this limit. Under Proposition 41, the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the limit.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Auditor Costs, Mostly Paid by New Revenues. Proposition 41 would increase State Auditor costs by creating new and ongoing audit requirements. The costs would depend on (1) the number of new or increased special taxes that are proposed and approved and (2) the complexity of the programs being audited. These costs likely would be in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time. The one-time and ongoing audit costs associated with special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature would be paid from the revenues collected by the special taxes. One-time audit costs associated with special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters would be paid from the state’s General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. Proposition 41 would require a summary of the State Auditor’s review to appear in the VIG when a voter initiative with a special tax appears on the ballot. These audit summaries could add several pages to the VIG, which would increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Possible Savings if State Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to make recommendations for programs to reduce costs or improve efficiency. Proposition 41 could result in savings or improved services if policymakers implement the State Auditor’s recommendations and those recommendations prove effective. Any resulting savings would depend on future decisions and are not known.
Net Effect Not Known. The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 41
CALIFORNIANS DESERVE BETTER RESULTS FOR OUR TAX DOLLARS
Prop. 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct independent public audits of programs funded by proposed new taxes in order to increase transparency and accountability and drive better outcomes.
Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country-on top of our high cost of living. This year alone, California’s state government will spend more than $350 billion-a 79% increase in spending since 2019. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it.
We deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop. 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Here’s how Prop. 41 works.
PUBLIC AUDITS TO PROVIDE ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND OVERSIGHT
Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs funded by new tax measures, with the results posted publicly. The audits must:
• Track all program spending and assess whether it’s achieving its intended outcomes; • Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability; • Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; • Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and programs made more effective.
Prop. 41 requires audits both before taxes are voted on to provide transparency to voters, and ongoing audits of programs funded by approved taxes to ensure accountability. PROP. 41: INDEPENDENT, PUBLIC INFORMATION FOR VOTERS ON PROPOSED TAXES
Before we vote on new taxes to fund programs, voters should have access to independent information about how those programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Under Prop. 41, the Auditor’s findings must be posted publicly and in the Voter Information Guide-so voters can make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
“This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending- ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known and may be cited as the
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency
in California Government Act of 2026.
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
The people of the State of California hereby find and
declare the following:
(a) Every day, Californians are facing an affordability
crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity, health care,
home and auto insurance, and many other life
necessities continue to escalate.
(b) Californians are already among the highest-taxed
people in the United States. A recent analysis by a
nonpartisan research institute concluded that
California ranks 48th in the nation in subjecting its
population to taxes, when considering individual
income taxes, sales taxes, property taxes, and other
forms of taxation. California has the highest state sales
tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.
(c) Public programs provide much-needed services,
including to children, families, and the most vulnerable
in our state. But billions of our tax dollars have flowed
into programs like homelessness efforts, with far too
little to show for it.
(d) Before asking taxpayers to pay even more of their
hard-earned money to support programs that are
ineffective, we must institute greater transparency and
trackable progress of program improvements to ensure
we stop funding failure and start funding successful
outcomes. Government must use our tax dollars more
wisely.
41 (e) Some of these efforts are already underway. For
example, the Newsom Administration has sought to
increase efficiency in government through greater
utilization of technology and automation, creation of an
Office of Data Innovation, and modernizing the
Department of Motor Vehicles. This is consistent with
earlier efforts President Obama undertook at the
federal level aimed at reducing waste in government
and cutting underperforming programs.
(f) However, while these existing efforts are a good
start, more should be done to reduce inefficiency and
cut government waste. For example, recent studies
have found that as much as 25 cents of every dollar in
some programs are lost to inefficiency or waste.
(g) Nonetheless, the Legislature and special interest
groups continue to propose new and higher taxes for
pet projects without doing the hard work of ensuring
that government programs are already using their
existing revenues as effectively and efficiently as
possible. Californians have a right to require that state
government improve the effectiveness and efficiency of
programs and cut waste before asking us to pay even
higher taxes—which just make our cost-of-living crisis
even worse.
148 | Text of Proposed Laws
(h) In 1979, California’s voters approved a state
spending cap to help check wasteful spending and
encourage more effective government—and to return
any excess revenues above the limit to taxpayers.
However, in the years since, special interests have
repeatedly passed new taxes that exempted
themselves from the state spending limit. This pushes
taxes even higher and makes it less likely that excessive
state revenues will be refunded to taxpayers.
(i) In order to ensure that state spending does not
spiral further out of control before the new efficiency
and transparency requirements of this act can have
their intended effect, we must prevent any new taxes
from being exempt from the state spending limit.
Protecting this voter-approved state spending limit is
critical for getting state government to be better
stewards of Californians’ tax dollars as intended by this
act. Government is more likely to spend taxpayer
dollars effectively and efficiently when government has
to live within its means under the state spending limit.
SEC. 3. Statement of Purpose.
In enacting this act, the purpose and intent of the
people of the State of California is to require the
California State Auditor to conduct upfront and ongoing
audits of all state programs that are targeted to receive
revenue from new or higher special taxes. The audits
must identify areas of potential savings and
improvements and the results must be shared with the
public in order to ensure that extra funding is actually
needed, that public programs are delivering results,
and that taxpayer dollars are not being lost to
inefficiency, waste, or abuse—while also prohibiting
exemptions from the state spending limit that forces
efficiency and discipline upon state government.

(a) When a certification for a proposed special tax

(2) Whether the program is maximizing its output for
every dollar spent.
(3) The extent to which the program is actually
achieving its intended goals and outcomes.

1. Does the Gann limit provision do real harm? Analysis: The Gann limit (Article XIII B) caps appropriations from tax revenues. Revenue above the limit must be returned to taxpayers (per Prop 111, the excess is allocated: half to schools as additional apportionment, half refunded). Excluding certain taxes from the limit (like Prop 30's millionaire tax? Actually Prop 30 revenues went into General Fund, so counted). Many special taxes are excluded — e.g., Prop 1A transportation tax? Actually the state's appropriations limit has been below revenue in recent years, so the constraint isn't currently binding, but if revenue exceeds it, it forces refunds/school spending.

Key point: Prop 41's Section 3(b) says the state "shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax" enacted on or after Jan 1, 2026 if exempted/excluded from the Gann limit. That is retroactive to Jan 1, 2026, and applies to all state taxes (not just special taxes) — that could invalidate existing taxes enacted in 2026 (e.g., any tax legislation passed in 2026 that directs revenue to a special fund). Let me check whether the 2026 Legislature enacted taxes excluded from the Gann limit. There may also be an issue with taxes that deposit revenues into special funds outside the General Fund — a very common structure. Many existing state taxes are like that (e.g., fuel excise taxes go into special funds, but are they counted in the appropriations limit? Actually the state's limit includes most tax proceeds; some are excluded, like gas tax? Hmm).

Note: This could have huge unintended consequences: any tax whose revenue goes to a fund outside the General Fund whose appropriations aren't counted would be prohibited from being imposed/collected. This is legally ambiguous and could create chaos for many taxes.

2. Audit requirements: The pre-election audit at 25% signature threshold imposes a burden — the State Auditor would need to audit programs for every proposed special tax initiative, even ones that never qualify. Cost borne by General Fund for failed ones. LAO says low millions per year. It could chill citizen initiatives (a burden on the initiative process). Also, "identify ways to cut costs 10%" is arbitrary. And the audit summary in the VIG could be used to shape voter opinion — arguably the Auditor is nonpartisan so it's fine, but it could be seen as politicizing the Auditor's office.

3. The measure is transparently designed as a poison pill for Prop 40, funded overwhelmingly by billionaires who would pay the tax (Brin >$100M, Schmidt $40M, Doerr $40M, etc.). Conflicts of interest.

4. Interaction: If Prop 41 gets more yes votes than Prop 40, all provisions of Prop 40 are null and void. Also, Prop 40 has its own conflicting-measures clause, which is oddly drafted: it says any measure that "levies a tax or affects the tax rates on net worth... of billionaires, or provides for use of funds from a tax on billionaire net worth" is in conflict. That doesn't clearly cover Props 41/42 (they don't levy a tax on billionaires). Actually, Prop 40's clause is one-directional: Prop 41 and 42 declare conflict with Prop 40. And the constitutional rule (Art. II, Sec. 10(b)) — when two measures conflict and both are approved, the one with the most yes votes prevails on conflicting provisions. So the outcome would depend on relative vote totals.

Also, arguably a "no" vote preserves the ability of wealthy interests to structure taxes outside the spending limit.

Arguments for NO: It's a poison-pill measure funded by billionaires with a direct financial stake; the audit provisions are largely redundant and burdensome (LAO and State Auditor already do this work; audits triggered at 25% signature collection is arbitrary and wasteful; cost falls on General Fund if the measure fails); the Gann limit provision would constrain the state's ability to raise revenue for needed programs far into the future, with unpredictable and potentially large consequences (could invalidate taxes already enacted in 2026 whose revenue goes to special funds), and would force refunds/school reallocations; it also would nullify Prop 40's health care funding if Prop 40 passes with fewer votes. Broad coalition of newspapers (SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times, LA Times?) recommend no; SPUR recommends no.

Also check the "Building a Better California" campaign finance and whether there's evidence the measure was drafted as a poison pill (Brin's statements). Summary
Proposition 41 would write two rules into the California Constitution. First, programs funded by new state special taxes would face independent audits by the state auditor. These audits would occur when the ballot initiative is initially proposed and then every four years after a special tax takes effect. Second, no new state tax could circumvent the Gann limit, the voter-approved spending cap adopted in 1979. Hoover Institution research shows that California’s spending has grown far faster than inflation or population and that the state budget rises and falls with the fortunes of a small number of high-income taxpayers. Proposition 41 is best read as an attempt to restore discipline to that budget. It also contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would void the billionaire tax on the same ballot (see California Decides, Prop 40: The Billionaire Tax Act (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)).
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0040A1).
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment.
A vote YES means: Starting retroactively on January 1, 2026, any program that would be the recipient of new or increased special tax revenues as a result of a citizen initiative must undergo state performance audits prior to the vote. Such programs, and those receiving revenues from legislatively enacted new or increased special taxes, must be audited every four years thereafter. No new state tax or increase to a state tax enacted on or after that date may route its revenue outside California’s voter-approved spending limit, commonly referred to as the Gann limit.
A vote NO means: California keeps current law. New special taxes are not subject to this audit regime, and new taxes may continue to direct revenue into funds that sit outside the Gann limit, as several existing taxes already do.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0040A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0040 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-040)
1. Overview
Proposition 41 would add a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. It has two main provisions.
The first provision is an audit requirement for programs that would receive funds from proposed special tax initiatives. A special tax is one whose revenue is dedicated to specific purposes rather than available for general use. When the proponents of a citizen initiative that would create a new or increased special tax notify the secretary of state that they have gathered 25 percent of the required signatures, the state auditor must begin a financial and performance audit of each program the special tax would fund. The audit must assess program effectiveness, evaluate the potential for fraud, waste, and abuse, and recommend ways the program could achieve budgetary savings of at least 10 percent a year. If the measure qualifies for the ballot, an executive summary of the audit must be printed in the state voter information guide.
A subsequent audit must be repeated every four years for every new or increased special tax enacted by the legislature or by voters on or after January 1, 2026. When a tax passes, the audit costs are reimbursed from the tax’s own revenue. When a tax initiative fails to qualify or is rejected, the general fund absorbs the cost.
The second provision protects the state spending limit from being circumvented by future state taxes. The Gann limit, adopted by voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and amended by Proposition 111 in 1990, caps how much tax revenue the state may appropriate each year. It’s adjusted for increases to population and per capita income, and some substantial categories of spending are excluded from the cap. According to the Gann limit, if tax revenue exceeds the limit over two consecutive years the excess revenue must be split between taxpayer rebates and additional K–14 school funding. For context, rapid tax revenue growth has rarely resulted in mandatory Gann limit rebates.
However, under current rules a new tax can be written to deposit its revenue in a fund that is excluded from the appropriations counted against the Gann limit. Proposition 41 would forbid that design for any state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative, but the ban is limited to taxes that take effect on or after January 1, 2026. New special taxes would still be permitted, but their revenue would simply count toward the same spending cap that applies to other nonexempt tax revenues.
The second provision connects Proposition 41 to Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act. If Prop 40 is approved it would route its revenue into a separate reserve fund that sits outside the structure of the Gann limit, the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee, and the rainy-day budget rules. Proposition 41 prohibits new or increased state taxes from circumventing the structure intended to limit the growth of California government spending, and it includes specific text that will nullify Proposition 40 if both initiatives pass but Proposition 41 receives more yes votes.
2. The legal language
Full text:
Initiative 25-0040A1, “The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf) (eight pages, amended language submitted January 12, 2026).
Key language:
“No state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 shall be exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation. The State of California shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 if the state tax is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation.”
What it amends: Adds a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. The article defines “Government Spending Limitation” as Article XIII B, the Gann limit, and defines an exempted tax as one whose revenue is deposited outside the general fund and left out of the appropriations subject to the limit or that raises the appropriations limit by statute.
Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it. The measure also includes a self-defense provision that appoints and funds independent counsel through a continuous general fund appropriation if the governor and attorney general decline to defend it.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
It would create constitutionally required audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes, both before a tax initiative reaches voters and every four years after a tax takes effect. It also creates a ban on excluding the revenue from any new or increased state tax from the Gann spending limit.
Where?
Statewide, written into the California Constitution.
When?
It takes effect on passage and reaches back to taxes enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026.
Why?
The initiative’s authors frame it as a response to California’s nation-leading tax rates and their effect on the state’s affordability crisis. The stated purpose is to require up-front, recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes and to prevent new taxes from circumventing the Gann limit so that surplus revenue is refunded rather than spent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
Audit requirements of Proposition 41 address a documented problem. For example, in 2024 the state auditor found that California spent roughly $24 billion on homelessness and housing programs over five fiscal years without consistently tracking whether the money reduced homelessness. Three of the five programs reviewed did not produce enough data to judge their cost-effectiveness at all. Proposition 41 would make that kind of review routine for programs funded by new special taxes, and it would give voters an audit summary before they vote on a tax initiative. Independent, recurring performance audits with concrete savings targets are the kind of accountability that good-government advocates across the spectrum have long sought.
Proposition 41’s requirement that future special taxes be subject to the Gann limit is similarly reasonable: California’s fiscal challenge is accelerated spending, not a shortage of revenue. Research by Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Lee Ohanian shows that from 2019 to 2023 California’s population fell by almost 500,000 people, while the state budget grew nearly 57 percent (31 percent after inflation). Additional research by Hoover fellows Lanhee J. Chen and Joshua D. Rauh describes how California’s heavy reliance on the personal income tax, which now supplies most general fund tax revenue, ties the budget to the performance of the stock market. In 2021, the top 10 percent of taxpayers paid almost 90 percent of personal income tax revenue. Meanwhile, the state budget swung $175 billion from a surplus in 2022 to a deficit in 2024.
The Gann limit is one of the few constitutional tools that restrains government spending growth during economic booms that becomes a fiscal catastrophe during leaner times. Prior analysis by Hoover Fellow Bill Whalen has traced how the Gann limit’s fiscal discipline has been eroded over time, from Proposition 111’s 1990 exclusion of new gas tax revenue to budgeting practices that kept billions out of the limit calculation. Proposition 41 would close the special-fund circumvention for any future tax.
Importantly, Prop 41 does not ban new taxes, nor does it cut existing programs. It simply requires that revenue from any new tax be counted alongside the rest of state spending, so that a future surplus is dedicated to a tax rebate and additional school funding (per Prop 4 and Prop 111) rather than accumulating in a dedicated fund. This rule should help encourage policymakers to be more thoughtful about expanding government programs when tax revenues unexpectedly increase.
Like Proposition 42, Proposition 41 contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would nullify Prop 40. This specificity is likely preferable to asking the courts to decide which parts of two conflicting constitutional amendments survive.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 41 would require any programs receiving funding from new or increased special taxes to be audited by the state auditor to assess performance, evaluate potential for waste, fraud, and abuse, and identify explicit cost savings opportunities. It would also require each new state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative to be subject to the Gann limit. Its most immediate effect would be to nullify Proposition 40 if it draws more yes votes, while its lasting effect would be to hold all future state taxes to the same spending cap as the rest of the budget.
Hoover Institution research shows that California’s fiscal problem is driven by spending increases that have managed to outstrip even the state’s strong tax revenue growth. From that perspective, Proposition 41 would offer increased oversight on how well California is spending taxpayer dollars.

Memorandum
To: Interested Parties
From: Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), and Darien
Shanske (UC Davis)1
Re: Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California’s Public Finance
Date: August 20, 2026
Introduction
In this memorandum, we will discuss the potential impacts of Propositions 41 and
42 on current and future initiatives and legislation, as well as on current California
Medicaid tax programs, starting with possible impacts on Proposition 3, the measure on
November’s ballot to extend personal income tax rate increases.
The purpose of the memo is to identify legal risks raised by the propositions that
prudent citizens should be aware of given the high stakes. We are not arguing how a court
should decide these issues and we do not claim that we are offering the best or most
persuasive legal arguments. We do, however, believe that there is a real risk courts could
reach these outcomes.
Our bottom line is that both propositions are poorly drafted in a manner that could
pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key
spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises. That is not
surprising. These are deceptive measures that were drafted quickly to trick voters that
support the billionaire wealth tax (Prop 40) into voting for competing measures that could
undermine that tax. The billionaire funders of these initiatives are acting with reckless
disregard for the collateral damage to California’s fiscal system and indeed they may even
benefit from weakening California’s existing taxes affecting the most wealthy.
Executive Summary
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the
teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners)
or invalidate it outright.
1 Institutional affiliations are listed for identification purposes only.
2
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other
revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have
many employees on Medi-Cal.
• The prohibition on easing the state appropriation limit in Proposition 41 could
undermine many existing and proposed taxes to fund California’s contributions to
Medi-Cal, including current MCO taxes and the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee
(HQAF).
• The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the
ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or
otherwise.
• The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any
future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for
financing a wide array of local services.
Proposition 41
Proposition 41 makes two significant changes to California law. First, it adds many
new audit requirements, specifically pre-election audits of programs that would receive
funds from a proposed special tax initiative; and recurring audits, every four years, of
programs receiving moneys from special taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026,
whether enacted by the Legislature or by initiative.2 Second, the proposition prohibits
collecting any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 that is exempted
or excluded from the appropriations limit of Article XIIIB, the so-called Gann limit, whether
the exemption comes from an outside-the-General-Fund special fund whose spending is
not counted or from raising the limit itself. Proposition 41, secs. 3, 4(b). The obvious point
of this second change, hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40.
But both changes would likely weaken California public finance by threatening California’s
ability to raise revenues and fund spending programs.
On the Merits
Prop 41 targets the primary (and, in many cases, the only plausible remaining) way
that state tax policy can be done and that state services can be adequately funded. Any
increase in taxes enacted by the Legislature requires a two-thirds supermajority of each
house.3 Statewide initiatives, by contrast, can raise taxes by majority vote. Not surprisingly,
most major tax policy changes over recent decades have therefore occurred via initiative.
Since voters are unlikely to support tax increases for unspecified purposes, the limits on
2 Prop. 41, Secs. 1, 2.
3 Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
3
measures adopting taxes for specified purposes tilts the deck against most of those
measures. Even if there were eventually an attempt to change Prop 41 through another
ballot measure, the pre-election audit requirement would still apply to any special tax
initiatives on that ballot.
The audits that Prop 41 would impose are slanted to make it more difficult to adopt
and fund new programs. Consider, for example, that a pre-election audit must consider:
“How the program's costs compare to any analogous programs in the non-government
sector”; and also: “Recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary
savings of at least 10% annually.” The audits would thus institutionalize a cost-cutting,
private-sector-comparison framework, and the executive summary of the pre-election
audit would be printed in the voter guide immediately after the Legislative Analyst’s
impartial analysis.4
In sum, every proposed special tax initiative would come before the voters bundled
with an official analysis oriented toward finding savings and private alternatives. These
expensive, burdensome and largely redundant5 requirements would hinder special tax
initiatives, making them more difficult to pass and less effective if passed.
The second provision regarding the Gann limit would double down on what has
proven to be a disastrous set of fiscal policies. The existing Gann limit works by capping
government expenditures over a given two-year period. Excess amounts must be split
between taxpayer rebates and education.6 The cap increases only to the extent of growth in
California population and cost of living.7 Given the increasing demands on the state
government, future uncertainties, and the changing nature of federal assistance, the limit
does not act so much as a ceiling as a vise squeezing out funds for core services.8 For
example, what happens if the state government needs to spend more on (say) wildfires? Or,
4 Sec. 1(e)(2).
5 California law is already full of audit requirements and indeed has a powerful and independent
state auditor (Govt Code 8543 et seq, see especially GC 8546.1) that issues regular,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/, and, often critical, reports about state operations. See, e.g.,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/reponses-2025-108-all/. And sometimes the state requires
particular audits. See, e.g., Bus. And Prof. Code 6145(b). As further discussed, the income tax
extensions authorized by Proposition 3 are already subject to audit. Art. XIII, Sec. 36(g).
6 Art. XIIIB, Sec. 2.
7 Art. XIIIB, Secs. 8(e), (f).
8 Making a similar point, here is Jason Sisney (an Assembly budget insider): “Therefore, if revenues
push the state to its Gann limit, non-Proposition 98 programmatic spending (such as annual tax-
supported spending on health and human services (HHS), housing, universities, prisons, state
employees and natural resources programs) probably would have to be cut more in this situation.”
https://jasonsisney.substack.com/p/state-moving-closer-to-its-appropriation
4
what if the state government must spend more to backfill vicious cuts from the federal
government?
The state has hit the Gann limit recently (2022) and is about $30 billion under the
Gann limit currently. Suppose Prop 3 passes without incident and the AI boom does lead to
substantial increases in revenue. At that point, the state will be close to the limit. Any
possible new initiatives for education, child care, housing or wildfire abatement could then
well go over the limit.
Threats to Proposition 3
The audit requirements of Proposition 41 arguably apply to Proposition 3 because
Proposition 3 would seem to impose a “special tax” enacted “by a statewide initiative
measure on or after January 1, 2026.” Sec. 2(a)(1). Proposition 3 makes permanent the
existing 1% tax surcharge on income above $1 million that is set to expire in 2030; all of its
revenues are earmarked primarily for education. It thus likely involves a “special tax,”
which is “a tax that can only be used to fund specific, as opposed to unlimited, purposes”
(according to Prop 41), because the Education Protection Account revenues added by Prop
3 may be used only for specified education and health care purposes. Sec. 4(d) of
Proposition 41; Article XIII, Sec. 36(e) of Proposition 3.
As for whether Proposition 3 was enacted after January 1, 2026, a court could
plausibly find that a tax first approved in 2012 is “enacted” in 2026 when the voters delete
its sunset. The new provision is different than the old in that it will never expire; the post-
2030 tax will exist only because of the 2026 vote; and the adoption of the extension is itself
literally an enactment.9
Thus, Proposition 41 might plausibly be interpreted by courts as applying to
Proposition 3. If so, Proposition 41 would require onerous and burdensome audits of the
programs it funds.
Further, if both measures pass and Proposition 41 receives more affirmative votes,
every provision of Proposition 3, including the rate extension itself, could be ruled void.
The terms of Proposition 41 state that it nullifies other conflicting 2026 initiatives if it
receives more votes. Prop 41 defines conflicting measures as “another initiative measure
9 Notably, neither Prop 41’s prohibition nor its grandfather clause discusses extensions, even
though California drafters know how to address extensions expressly. For instance, Proposition 218
reaches taxes that governments “impose, extend, or increase,” and the Proposition 218
implementation statute treats removal of a sunset as an extension. Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(b); Gov. Code
Sec. 53750(e).
5
that …imposes different audit rules on special taxes.” Sec. 5(a). Proposition 3 carries
forward Proposition 30’s audit rules, and those rules are different from Proposition 41’s.10
Threats to the MCO Tax
The sloppy drafting of Proposition 41 implicates policies far beyond Proposition 3.
We will briefly consider spending on health care.
Start with the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax, which California expects to
generate as much as $8 billion annually in federal matching funds. There are now arguably
two separate MCO provisions that will take effect after 2026 authorization, both of them
threatened by Prop 41.
The first is SB 125, enacted in June 2026, which imposes a tax of $8.85 per enrollee
per month for 2027 through 2029 and deposits the proceeds in the new Medi-Cal Stability
Fund, dedicated to specified Medi-Cal purposes.11 SB 125 is a special tax enacted after
January 1, 2026, so under Prop 41 each Medi-Cal program receiving its moneys would face
recurring State Auditor financial and performance audits, with the private-sector
comparisons and ten percent savings recommendations, and with the Auditor reimbursed
from the tax revenues themselves.12 As explained above, this would be very burdensome
and problematic. And because the Stability Fund broadly co-funds managed care payments
and rates, there is a further risk that a court would rule that the auditable “programs”
include major portions of Medi-Cal managed care, rather than just the marginal SB 125
dollars. Thus Prop 41 could require the state to pay for audits recommending how to
privatize Medi-Cal and slash it by 10%.
Proposition 41 also deprives the state of flexibility to keep SB 125 effective in the
future. As enacted, the SB 125 tax uses up capacity under the Gann limit, narrowing room
for other revenue needs. SB 125 also sunsets in 2030, at a time when there might not be
room under the Gann limit available for renewal. In both cases, the state could be left
choosing between crowding out other priorities under the limit or losing the tax—and the
10 Indeed, on one point the two measures give seemingly incompatible commands about the same
dollars. Proposition 41 provides that the State Auditor “shall be reimbursed from the revenue
generated by the special tax” for the reasonable costs of its audits. Sec. 2(d). Section 36 (Proposition
3), however, provides that moneys deposited in the Education Protection Account for education
“shall not be used to pay any costs incurred by the Legislature, the Governor, or any agency of state
government,” and it separately bars using Account funds for administrative costs. Art. XIII, Sec.
36(e)(5), (6).
11 Ch. 24, Stats. 2026 (SB 125), adding a new Article 7.2 to the Welfare and Institutions Code; the
new tax is expressly made not subject to Proposition 35's chapter. See Dept. of Finance, Manual of
State Funds, Fund 3492 (Medi-Cal Stability Fund classified as included).
12 Sec. 2.
6

implications for state funding of Medi-Cal.
In addition, in 2024, Proposition 35 implemented a permanent MCO tax starting in
2027.13 Proposition 35 also used a provision of the Gann limit, Art. XIIIB, Sec. 4, to lift the
ceiling for four years in order to accommodate the new spending.14 Recall that Prop 41
prohibits collecting any tax that modifies the Gann limit if the tax takes effect on or after
January 1, 2026. 15 There is thus a significant risk Prop 41 would prevent Proposition 35
from taking effect.
Threats to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF)
Prop 41 could also bar modifications to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF),
including modifications that might be required by the federal government in order for the
HQAF to remain in effect. The HQAF draws down billions of dollars in federal matching
funds for hospital payments, and the federal government approved the 2025 program in
June 2026. HQAF funds are exempt from the Gann limit.16 A court might conclude that an
HQAF modified after January 1, 2026 “takes effect” after that date for purposes of Prop 41.
That would prevent California from modifying or improving the HQAF, even if required by
federal rule changes, such as those now pending. A Trump or other hostile HHS aware of
this dilemma might go out of its way to require HQAF changes that it knows California
cannot implement.17
We expect that California would argue the HQAF is not subject to Prop 41 limits
because it is a “fee,” not a “tax,” but a court might well rule otherwise. This is because
Proposition 41 does not define “state tax” and because California generally interprets
“taxes” quite broadly. See Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(b). A multibillion dollar charge that funds not
only services for the payors but also transfers to others, as the HQAF does, will be quite
likely to face a plausible challenge that it constitutes a tax and not a fee.
Note that the stakes of these threats are further magnified because the statute
makes it so that the hospital fee becomes inoperative if a lawsuit is filed and a preliminary

14 Proposition 35, Sec. 2.
15 Prop. 41, Secs. 3, 4(b)(2).
16 Cal. Const., art. XVI, § 3.5(d); Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds (Hospital Quality Assurance
Revenue Fund classified as excluded from the state appropriations limit). The Finance fund record
predates Proposition 52 and is based on the notion that the revenues are not proceeds of taxes;
Proposition 52 is the source of the constitutional exclusion.
17 It could also be argued that the HQAF takes effect after Jan. 1, 2026 even if it is not modified after
that date. This is because its mechanics operate through discrete, numbered program periods, and
each of these has its own fee model and its own federal approval. Thus, a period beginning after
January 1, 2026 could well be characterized as the tax taking effect after that date.
7

General Fund cost.18 A qualifying preliminary injunction or other order could thus obstruct
the program well before any final judgment, even if the challenge might ultimately fail on
the merits.
Threats to the Skilled Nursing Facility Fees
Yet another health funding source at risk from Proposition 41 is the skilled nursing
facility quality assurance fee (SNF-QAF). Like the HQAF, this is a provision intended to
generate federal matching funds, and it is expected to bring in several billion dollars over
the next 5 years. The SNF-QAF was extended by the Legislature in July 2026 through the
end of 2027,19 and its revenues are also classified as exempt from the Gann limit. Thus, a
court could well decide based on these arguments that collection of the fee should be
barred, thereby cutting off the federal matching funds and supplemental payments to
nursing facilities that the program exists to generate.
Single-Subject Threats
It is also possible that Prop 41 could make it impossible for any future initiative to
be exempt from the Gann limit, yoking California to the fiscal system of the distant 1970s in
perpetuity. The California Constitution requires that an initiative “embracing more than
one subject” may not be submitted to the voters or have any effect.20 Because Proposition
41's restrictions would be added to the Constitution (if they pass), a future revenue
measure could escape the restrictions only by pairing its new tax with a constitutional
override of Proposition 41. This thus gives opponents of any future revenue measure a
powerful new tool for challenging such measures through litigation. That is, future
initiatives would have to have what are arguably two subjects: their own goals, and also
disabling the Prop 41 rules.
It might be objected in regard to this that provisions suspending Prop 41 rules that
would frustrate a future initiative are part of a single subject, much as today many

added as to the Gann limit. Arguably, a court could find that these are two separate subjects
that would require two separate measures. Although California’s single-subject test is

Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits For New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Tax Audits, One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative.
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026
The Transparency Act
Summary
Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0041A (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20%28Gov.%20Efficiency%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures. The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%. If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.
Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of these audits will be reimbursed using revenue generated from the new tax if voters approve the measure. If a special tax initiative fails, the state general fund covers the audit costs.
It would also prohibit the state from enforcing any new tax enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026, that is exempted or excluded from the state spending limit.
Proposition 41 conflicts directly with Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) (the Billionaire Wealth Tax initiative). If both pass, whichever measure receives more "yes" votes will prevail in its entirety. Because Proposition 40 excludes its revenues from the state spending limit, Proposition 41 would render Proposition 40 unenforceable if Proposition 41 wins more votes.
Note about the Gann Limit: Approved by California voters in 1979 asProposition 4 (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/ca_ballot_props/864/), the Gann Limit restricts how much tax revenue state and local governments (including school districts) can spend each year, adjusted annually for population changes and economic growth. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes (unrestricted funds for general government operations) and special taxes (funds earmarked for specific purposes), though certain spending categories—such as infrastructure and emergency response—are exempt. (Sources: California Budget Center, What is the Gann Limit? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians) , Gann Limit (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gann_Limit) , CA Department of Finance, Description of (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf)Fund Classifications in the Treasury (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf))
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. However, the State Auditor costs will increase due to the new and ongoing work to carry out the audit requirements in this measure.
Due to additional pages of audit information being included in the voter information guides could increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative on the ballot.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
YES: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
